analysis.one_liner: Narrows the federal definition of "employee," reclassifying many workers as independent contractors outside wage and overtime protections.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have narrowed who counts as an employee under federal wage and overtime law, was introduced with four Senate Republicans and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Fair Labor Standards Act so that someone counts as an "employee" only under the common law test — basically, whether the employer controls what work is done and how it is done [S2][S3]. Today the law uses a broader standard, under which many workers who depend on a company for their livelihood count as employees entitled to minimum wage and overtime. Under this bill, many of those workers — including many app-based gig workers — would instead be independent contractors with no federal minimum wage or overtime rights [S2][S3]. The bill never advanced past its initial committee referral and died when the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that use or depend on independent contractor classifications gain the most. App-based gig platforms, delivery companies, staffing firms, franchisors, and other employers would find it harder for workers to count as employees under the Fair Labor Standards Act, reducing their exposure to minimum wage, overtime, and payroll obligations and to misclassification lawsuits [S2][S3]. Some workers who genuinely operate as independent businesses and want to keep contractor status would also benefit from a single, clearer federal test [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gig platforms and businesses using contractors

how_it_helps.text: It gives businesses a narrower, more predictable test for who counts as an employee: under the common law rules, an individual is an employee mainly when the employer controls what work is done and how it is done.
It amends the Fair Labor Standards Act's employee definition to use the 'usual common law rules', moving away from the broader standard courts currently apply.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who would be reclassified as independent contractors pay the cost: they would lose federal minimum wage and overtime protections and bear business expenses, tax withholding, and benefits costs themselves [S2][S3]. Law-abiding employers who currently classify those workers as employees would face competitive pressure from rivals using the narrower classification.

drawbacks.text: The bill would reclassify many currently covered workers as independent contractors, stripping them of federal minimum wage and overtime protections, with no replacement safeguards for misclassified workers.

Switching from the broader 'suffer or permit' standard to the common law control test narrows coverage by design: a worker who depends on one company for their income but does not have their hours and methods directed would fall outside the FLSA entirely.

Supporters' strongest argument is that overlapping federal tests (economic realities, ABC tests in some states) make compliance unpredictable and expose businesses using genuinely independent contractors to costly litigation; a single common law standard would be clearer. The honest cost of that clarity is that workers misclassified under the looser standard lose protections they currently hold.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated appeal is consistency: replacing multiple overlapping federal tests with one familiar control-based standard would give businesses clear rules and match the definition used in tax law. But the design does most of its work in one direction — the common law test classifies fewer people as employees than the standards currently used under the FLSA, so the practical effect is fewer workers covered by minimum wage, overtime, and related protections. The flexibility some independent workers value could be preserved by narrower carve-outs or a safe harbor for genuine contractors; this bill instead rewrites the baseline for everyone. The cost to workers' pay protections is substantial, and the bill never received a hearing where those trade-offs could be examined.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Scott introduced the bill on March 2, 2021, with three Republican cosponsors: Sens. Blackburn, Braun, and Cramer.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died there when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that benefit from classifying workers as independent contractors, and workers who keep their current federal wage protections because the narrower definition never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Contractor-reliant businesses; workers kept current protections

for.name: Sen. Tim Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to replace the FLSA's employee definition with the common law control test.

for.name: Sens. Marsha Blackburn, Mike Braun, and Kevin Cramer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; 3 of 50 Senate Republicans signed on and no Democrat or Independent did.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it received no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat or Independent signed on, and the bill never advanced past referral in the Democratic-controlled Senate.

industries.note: A narrower employee definition makes it easier to treat drivers and couriers as independent contractors, avoiding minimum wage, overtime, and payroll obligations for large workforces. Workers who lose those protections bear the cost.

industries.industry: Staffing, franchising, and other businesses that rely on contractor classification
industries.note: These employers face fewer wage-and-hour obligations and lower exposure to misclassification lawsuits when fewer workers count as employees. The savings come out of workers' pay protections.

industries.industry: Hourly and gig workers depending on minimum wage and overtime protections
industries.note: Workers shifted to independent-contractor status lose federal minimum wage, overtime, and related Fair Labor Standards Act protections. This is the population the law was written to cover.
